paper_metadata.title: Quantum computational finance: Monte Carlo pricing of financial derivatives

summary: The paper proposes a gate‑based quantum Monte Carlo algorithm for pricing derivatives using amplitude estimation, achieving theoretical sample complexity O(1/ε) compared to classical Monte Carlo O(1/ε²). A classical simulation of the phase‑estimation subroutine for a European call option (S0=$100, K=$50, r=0.05, σ=0.2, T=1) shows error scaling with exponent −0.982 versus −0.5 classically, consistent with the predicted quadratic improvement.

experiments.description: Quantum Monte Carlo pricing of a European call option using amplitude estimation on a discretized Black-Scholes-Merton Brownian motion distribution.

algorithm.variant: Quantum Monte Carlo with amplitude estimation / phase estimation

hyperparameters.amplitude_estimation_success_probability: at least 8/π^2 for a single run; boosted by median of D runs

algorithm.parameter_initialization: State preparation via Grover-Rudolph distribution loading; phase estimation uses a known phase derived from the analytical option price in the numerical simulation section

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Brownian motion distribution discretized on n qubits; payoff encoded by controlled rotation on an ancilla qubit after computing discretized call payoff values
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate Π = e^{-rT} E_Q[max(0, S_T - K)] via amplitude estimation

problem_instance.description: European call option under the Black-Scholes-Merton model
problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Discretize Gaussian Brownian motion on a finite interval [−xmax, xmax] with 2^n points; approximate payoff function with n-bit fixed-point arithmetic
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Classical numerical simulations comparing quantum phase-estimation scaling against classical Monte Carlo; confidence matched to >99.5% using D ≈ 24 independent phase-estimation runs

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Analytical Black-Scholes price Π = $10.5 used to compute the phase θ = 2 arccos(1 − 2Π/S0) for the single-qubit phase estimation simulation
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Estimate option price from measured phase / ancilla probability; discount by e^{-rT}

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: error scaling reported as power law; fitted quantum slope ζQ = -0.982

speedup_claims.conditions: assuming efficient state preparation and payoff evaluation; for bounded-variance mean estimation and additive error epsilon
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports an almost quadratic empirical scaling in simulation (fitted quantum exponent -0.982) and a theoretical upper bound of -1; the asymptotic claim is in terms of sample complexity O(1/epsilon) vs O(1/epsilon^2).

speedup_claims.conditions: numerical simulation for a european call option with S0 = 100, K = 50, r = 0.05, sigma = 0.2, T = 1, D = 24
speedup_claims.caveats: This is inferred from fitted exponents zeta_Q = -0.982 and zeta_C = -0.5; the paper describes it as almost quadratic.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: ˜O(λ/ϵ) applications of U for bounded-variance mean estimation; quadratic improvement over classical Monte Carlo
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O(1/ϵ^2) samples for Monte Carlo estimation

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not quantified; paper only shows asymptotic scaling improvement (O(1/ε) vs O(1/ε²)) without constant-factor resource estimates.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Requires efficient state preparation of the risk‑neutral distribution, reversible payoff circuits, and large-scale fault‑tolerant amplitude estimation with repeated controlled-Q operations.
limiting_factors: Large reversible arithmetic circuits for payoff computation
No concrete qubit or gate estimates for realistic financial portfolios
Current hardware cannot implement deep controlled-Q phase estimation circuits

notes: No actual QPU is used; the paper states the phase-estimation subroutine can be simulated with Strawberry Fields / ProjectQ, so hardware is inferred as simulator_other.
The paper does not give a concrete qubit count for the numerical experiment; n depends on discretization, so num_qubits is left null/inferred as not specified.
Circuit depth is not explicitly quantified, so left null.
Authors explicitly claim a quadratic quantum speedup in Monte Carlo sample complexity using amplitude estimation.
However, the paper only demonstrates scaling numerically via classical simulation of phase estimation and provides no hardware experiment.

experiments.description: Quantum Monte Carlo pricing of an arithmetic Asian call option using amplitude estimation with multi-time-step Brownian path preparation.

algorithm.variant: Quantum Monte Carlo with amplitude estimation for Asian options

hyperparameters.distribution_preparation: Grover-Rudolph state preparation for each time step
hyperparameters.median_repetitions: D ≈ 24 in numerical phase-estimation discussion (applied generally to the quantum algorithm)

algorithm.parameter_initialization: Prepare L copies of the Gaussian increment state |p_Δt⟩ and sequentially compute the path-dependent average payoff

problem_formulation.encoding_details: L Gaussian increment registers, each discretized on m qubits; path label |j1,...,jL⟩ mapped to stock path and average payoff register
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate Π = e^{-rT} E_Q[max(0, A_T - K)] for arithmetic Asian option

problem_instance.description: Arithmetic Asian call option under the Black-Scholes-Merton model

dataset_specification.description: Equal time spacing Δt = T/L; stock path generated from Gaussian Brownian increments

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Discretize each Brownian increment on m qubits; compute stock path recursively in the log domain or price domain; compute arithmetic average along the path
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Theoretical resource discussion; no separate numerical Asian-option benchmark reported

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Prepare product state of L Gaussian increment distributions; compute stock path and running average classically within reversible arithmetic circuit
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Measure ancilla probability and discount to obtain option price

speedup_claims.conditions: arithmetic asian option pricing under the black-scholes-merton model with bounded-variance mean estimation and efficient reversible arithmetic
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper gives a theoretical resource analysis and states a similar speedup via Theorem 3; no separate numerical Asian-option benchmark is reported.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Similar ˜O(λ/ϵ) scaling via amplitude estimation / mean estimation with bounded variance

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not analyzed; only asymptotic scaling arguments provided.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Would require L Gaussian increment registers (Lm qubits) plus registers for stock path computation, averaging, and ancilla rotation, all within a fault-tolerant amplitude estimation framework.
limiting_factors: Large number of qubits needed for multi-step Brownian paths
Deep reversible arithmetic circuits for path simulation and averaging
State preparation overhead repeated for each time step

notes: The paper discusses the Asian-option circuit and resource scaling theoretically, but does not give a concrete qubit count for a specific numerical run; num_qubits is therefore left null.
No hardware platform is specified because this is a theoretical resource analysis, not an execution on a device.
Section VI provides only a theoretical construction for Asian options without numerical or hardware experiments.
